questions.text: Essential question: You have heard the basic 12-bar blues before. What do you think jazz musicians might have changed about the form to make it more interesting harmonically? Write 2-3 sentences of your first instinct. No wrong answer yet.

This module I will (a) identify jazz blues substitutions in bars 2, 9-10, and 11-12, (b) build a blues scale from any root and name the blue note, (c) explain call-and-response structure in a blues melody. Check that you have seen these goals.

answers.text: I have read this module's goals.

questions.text: How familiar are you with the 12-bar blues right now?
The jazz blues substitution in bar 2 of a basic blues in F is called the:
In a jazz blues in F, the quick-change chord in bar 2 is:
The ii-V substitution in bars 9-10 of a jazz blues in F replaces:
A "turnaround" in the 12-bar blues refers to:

answers.text: a progression in bars 11-12 that cycles the form back to bar 1
a cadence that ends the piece
a rhythmic pattern under the vocal melody

questions.text: The blues scale is best described as:

answers.text: the minor pentatonic scale plus the flat 5 (blue note)
the major scale with a lowered third
the whole-tone scale with an added pitch

questions.text: In the F blues scale (F-Ab-Bb-B-C-Eb), the blue note is:
The characteristic tension of blues melody comes from:

answers.text: playing major pitches over minor harmony
playing minor-scale pitches (especially flat 3 and flat 7) over major harmony

questions.text: In call-and-response blues form, the instrumental "response" typically fills:
"Blue notes" in blues and jazz refer to:

answers.text: flat 3, flat 5, and flat 7 used expressively over major harmony
the notes of the major scale
the notes of a dominant seventh chord

questions.text: True/False: In the basic 12-bar blues (before jazz substitutions), bar 2 stays on the I7 chord.
Your teacher has linked a Delta blues recording (solo guitar and voice, for example, a public-domain field recording or a similar solo performance). Listen to the excerpt, then identify the ensemble:

answers.text: a full blues band with drums and bass

questions.text: Your teacher has linked a Chicago electric blues recording (full amplified band, for example, a Muddy Waters-style track). Listen to the excerpt, then identify the ensemble:

answers.text: a full amplified blues band (guitar, bass, drums, harmonica)

questions.text: Essential question revisited: Jazz musicians added substitutions to the blues form. In your own words, explain what the three jazz-blues substitutions do and why each one adds harmonic interest.
How confident are you now building a blues scale and identifying the blue note?
What is the "quick change" in jazz blues, and in which bar does it appear?

This module practiced creativity within constraints (the 12-bar form is a fixed container; jazz musicians found ways to make it fresh). Name one other area of life where a fixed rule or structure pushes people to be more creative, not less.

Essential question: Why does rock music make you want to tap your foot or nod your head, while classical music usually does not produce the same physical reaction? Write 2-3 sentences of your first instinct. No wrong answer yet.

This module I will (a) explain the backbeat (accents on beats 2 and 4) and contrast it with on-beat emphasis, (b) notate and clap the tresillo (3+3+2) pattern, (c) identify at least two syncopation types in a pop song. Check that you have seen these goals.

answers.text: I have read this module's goals.

questions.text: How confident are you identifying the backbeat in a song right now?
The "backbeat" in rock and pop refers to:
Which instrument most commonly plays the backbeat in a rock drum kit?
"On-beat emphasis" (accents on beats 1 and 3) is most characteristic of:
The tresillo groups eight eighth notes as:
In the tresillo (3+3+2) pattern, the three accented eighth notes are:
The tresillo pattern originated in:
An "anticipation" in pop syncopation means a note arrives:

answers.text: one eighth note early, before the beat it harmonically belongs to

questions.text: "Metric displacement" in pop syncopation means:

answers.text: a phrase begins on an unexpected beat, creating the impression the meter shifted
a note arrives one eighth note early
a note repeats on the off-beat

questions.text: The "groove" in pop and R&B refers to:

answers.text: the repeating rhythmic pattern in the rhythm section that anchors the song's feel
the key signature of the song
the chord progression of the chorus

questions.text: True/False: Removing the backbeat (snare on 2 and 4) from a rock song would make it sound more like a march or classical piece.
Essential question revisited: Why does the backbeat make you want to move? Revise your opening answer now that you have analyzed the backbeat, tresillo, and syncopation patterns.
How confident are you now identifying the backbeat and tresillo in a song?
What is the tresillo pattern, and name one genre where you regularly hear it.

This module practiced attention to detail (hearing where the accent lands, not just hearing that rhythm exists). Name one other situation in life where noticing exactly where something happens makes a difference.

Essential question: Western music uses 12 equally-spaced pitches per octave. Have you ever heard music from another culture that seemed to use different, "in-between" pitches, pitches that do not exist on a piano? Describe what it sounded like. No wrong answer.

This module I will (a) compare Indian raga, Arabic maqam, and Western modes as parallel modal frameworks, (b) explain what a quarter tone is and why a piano cannot play one, (c) listen to a non-Western example and describe its scale structure. Check that you have seen these goals.

answers.text: I have read this module's goals.

questions.text: How familiar are you with music from outside the Western classical and pop traditions right now?
A "modal framework" is best described as:

answers.text: any system that organizes pitches into a scale with characteristic melodic tendencies and emotional associations
the specific Western system of seven diatonic modes
a rhythmic pattern used in non-Western music

questions.text: A "quarter tone" is:

answers.text: an interval half the size of a semitone, used in Arabic and Turkish music
a note held for a quarter of a beat

questions.text: Why can a standard piano not produce a quarter tone?

answers.text: because it has too few keys
because it uses only black and white keys
because it is tuned to equal temperament with 12 fixed pitches per octave, and quarter tones fall between those pitches
because the sustain pedal prevents it

questions.text: Indian raga specifies, beyond the pitches to use:

answers.text: ascending scale, descending scale, characteristic phrases, emotional content (rasa), and often a time of day
only the key signature and tempo

questions.text: The "rasa" in Indian raga refers to:

answers.text: the emotional content or mood associated with a specific raga
the rhythmic cycle (tala) underlying the performance
the tuning system of the ensemble
the number of pitches in the raga

questions.text: Arabic maqam uses how many distinct named modes?
Indonesian gamelan uses which two tuning systems?
Western equal temperament (12 equal pitches per octave) was standardized approximately when?
Which statement about world pitch systems is most accurate?

answers.text: Western equal temperament is the pitch system all cultures eventually converge on
no pitch system is inherently more 'natural' than another; what sounds natural is shaped by exposure
non-Western scales are less mathematically precise
Western modes are used by more people worldwide than any other system

questions.text: True/False: The ascending and descending versions of an Indian raga must use the same pitches in both directions.
Essential question revisited: Before this module, did non-Western scales sound "in tune" or "out of tune" to you? Has your thinking changed? Explain using at least one specific term from the lesson.
How confident are you now explaining the difference between raga, maqam, and Western modes?
What is a quarter tone, and name one tradition that uses it.

This module practiced intellectual humility (reconsidering what you assumed was "natural" or "correct"). Describe one area outside music where you have had to revise something you thought was obvious.
Essential question: What do you expect music to feel like when harmony avoids the familiar dominant-to-tonic pull? Write 2-3 sentences of your first instinct. No wrong answer yet.

In this module I will (a) build whole-tone and octatonic scales from any starting pitch, (b) explain the symmetrical properties of these collections, (c) identify whole-tone or octatonic harmonies in a public domain Impressionist score. Check that you have seen these goals.

answers.text: I have read this module's goals.

questions.text: How familiar are you with scales that use non-standard step patterns (like whole-tone or diminished scales)?
The whole-tone scale is built entirely of:
How many notes does a whole-tone scale contain?
How many unique transpositions of the whole-tone scale exist?
The whole-tone scale generates which type of triad?
The octatonic scale alternates:
The octatonic scale is also called the:
How many notes does an octatonic scale contain?
The octatonic scale repeats identically when transposed by a:
Which composer is most associated with using whole-tone scales to create coloristic, non-functional harmony?
True/False: Both the whole-tone and octatonic scales have a unique leading tone that creates a strong pull to a tonal center.
Essential question revisited: Now that you have built and analyzed whole-tone and octatonic scales, what makes a piece feel harmonically "weightless"? Revise your opening answer.
How confident are you constructing a whole-tone scale from any starting pitch?
How confident are you constructing an octatonic scale from any starting pitch?
In your own words, what does "symmetrical" mean for a scale, and why does symmetry eliminate the sense of a tonal center? (1-2 sentences.)
This module practiced precision (exact step patterns matter). Name one other field where a precise sequence or pattern produces a completely different result if even one step is wrong.
Essential question: When you hear music that has no clear home key or no V-I cadences, how does it feel? Write 2-3 sentences about your first instinct.

This module I will (a) describe major movements in 20th-century classical music: Impressionism, Neoclassicism, Expressionism, and Minimalism, (b) identify the compositional approach (pitch collection, serial, or tonal) of a given excerpt, (c) name two composers and describe their characteristic style. Check that you have seen these goals.

answers.text: I have read this module's goals.

questions.text: How familiar are you with the names Impressionism, Expressionism, Neoclassicism, or Minimalism in music?
Impressionism in music is associated with:

answers.text: Clear V-I cadences and strong tonal centers
Coloristic harmony, whole-tone scales, and avoidance of strong cadences
Gradual repetitive processes and static harmony

questions.text: Which composers are most closely associated with Impressionism?
Expressionism used:

answers.text: Classical forms like sonata and concerto
Minimal pitch material and gradual change

questions.text: Serialism organizes music using:

answers.text: A tone row of all 12 pitches in fixed order

questions.text: Neoclassicism is best described as:

answers.text: Rejecting all structure and embracing chaos
Returning to Classical forms with modern harmonic language

questions.text: Which movement reacted against the complexity of high modernism by using very few pitches and gradual change?
Steve Reich and Philip Glass are composers associated with:
According to OMT, the first step in analyzing post-tonal music is to:

answers.text: Identify the pitch collection being used

questions.text: Debussy and Ravel's works are considered public domain because:

answers.text: They gave permission for free use
They were published by a government agency

questions.text: True/False: In serial music, some pitches are more important than others because they function as tonal centers.
Essential question revisited: Now that you know the movements, how would you describe music that has no clear tonal center? Revise or expand the answer you wrote at the start of the module.
How confident are you matching a composer to their movement (Impressionism, Expressionism, Neoclassicism, or Minimalism)?
How confident are you identifying whether a piece uses a pitch collection vs. a tone row vs. tonal harmony?
In one sentence each, describe Serialism and Minimalism.

This module practiced curiosity (engaging with unfamiliar music without dismissing it). Name one other situation where approaching something unfamiliar with curiosity, rather than immediate judgment, would make a difference.

Essential question: You are about to analyze a piece of music using the tools of form, harmony, rhythm, and culture. What do you think it means to "analyze" a piece of music? Write 2-3 sentences of your first instinct.

This module I will: (a) apply form, harmonic, rhythmic, and cultural context analysis to a complete piece (b) create a listening score timeline diagram (c) write a practice integrated analysis essay Check that you have seen these goals.

answers.text: I have read and understood all three goals listed above.

questions.text: How confident are you right now applying more than one type of musical analysis to the same piece?
Integrated analysis means combining which of the following into a single analytical statement?

answers.text: formal, harmonic, rhythmic analysis, and cultural context
key signature identification and note reading

questions.text: A listening score is best described as...

answers.text: a published score purchased from a music publisher
a self-made timeline diagram of a piece's formal sections and key events
a graded essay about musical style
a recording of a live performance

questions.text: Which of the following is a chord schema you might identify in a pop or world music analysis?
In an integrated analysis essay, "cultural context" means...

answers.text: the number of instruments in the ensemble
the key signature of the piece
the tempo marking in the score
the historical, social, and stylistic background that gives the music meaning beyond the notes

questions.text: Tresillo is best described as...

answers.text: a chord quality found in jazz
a syncopated rhythmic pattern common in Latin music: long-short-long (3+3+2 in 8 subdivisions)
a form type found in baroque music

questions.text: In a pop or world music analysis, which analytical dimension asks you to identify the meter and note any groove patterns?
A listening score should mark which of the following? (Choose the BEST answer.)

answers.text: every note and rest in the piece
only the parts the analyst finds interesting
section boundaries with timestamps, section labels, and at least one harmony or texture note per section

questions.text: In the recommended essay structure for integrated analysis, what goes in the CONCLUSION paragraph?

answers.text: the names of all instruments in the ensemble
a list of every chord in the piece
connecting all analytical elements (form, harmony, rhythm, texture, culture) in 2-3 sentences
a new analysis of a different piece

questions.text: True or False: When analyzing a piece that is not in standard Western notation, it is not possible to do harmonic analysis.
Which of the following is an example of a cultural context statement in an analysis essay?

answers.text: The piece is in D minor with a harmonic minor scale.
The rhythm uses a 6/8 meter with consistent dotted-quarter groove.
The form follows an AABA structure with a 32-bar chorus.
This piece emerged from the West African griot tradition, where the kora serves as a storytelling instrument passed through family lineages.

questions.text: Essential question revisited: Revise your opening answer. What does it mean to "analyze" a piece of music? How has this module changed your definition?
How confident are you now applying integrated analysis to a piece of music?
Name one thing you marked on your listening score that surprised you or that you would not have noticed without the analysis framework.

This module practiced diligence (doing systematic, careful work even when it is difficult). Name one area outside music where systematic analysis helps you understand something you would otherwise miss.

quizzes.title: Module 25 Intro: What Do You Already Hear?

questions.text: Essential question: Think of a pop song you know well. Without looking it up, write down every section of the song in order as best you can. What labels would you give each section?

This module I will: (a) Map the formal sections of a pop song from memory after listening (b) Identify the function of each section (verse, chorus, pre-chorus, bridge) (c) Compare two songs that use the same form schema but sound completely different Confirm that you have seen these goals.

answers.text: I have read and seen these three goals.
I have not read these goals yet.

questions.text: How confident are you identifying the different sections of a pop song right now?
The standard verse-chorus form template in pop music is:

answers.text: Intro - Verse 1 - Chorus - Verse 2 - Chorus - Bridge - Chorus - Outro

questions.text: The chorus differs from the verse most importantly because the chorus:

answers.text: Uses the same lyrics and melody every time it appears
Only appears once in the song
Is always shorter than the verse

questions.text: The function of a pre-chorus is:

answers.text: To provide the final emotional climax
To build energy and harmonic anticipation before the chorus arrives
To repeat the verse with different instrumentation

questions.text: According to OMT (p. 598), the chorus is typically MORE harmonically ___ than the verse.
The bridge in a pop song typically:

answers.text: Occurs multiple times throughout the song
Provides contrast at a different register, texture, or harmony before the final chorus

questions.text: In pop song form, the verse's primary function is:

answers.text: To advance the narrative with changing lyrics each time

questions.text: What does a pre-chorus typically use harmonically to build toward the chorus?

answers.text: The tonic chord (I) held for a long time
Harmonically unstable chords such as IV, ii, or V-area chords

questions.text: Two pop songs can use the SAME formal template but sound completely different because:

answers.text: The form template actually changes from song to song
Only one of them can have a chorus
Melody, harmony, lyrics, arrangement, and production choices create individuality within a shared form
Bridges are optional and make the songs different

questions.text: When doing form analysis from listening, which of the following is MOST important to mark?

answers.text: The section boundary timestamps and section function labels

questions.text: True or False: The outro of a pop song always repeats the chorus exactly as it appeared earlier in the song.

quizzes.title: Module 25 Outro: What Do You Hear Now?

questions.text: Essential question revisited: Now that you have mapped two songs, revise your opening answer: what is a "section" in a pop song, and what makes each section's function distinct?
How confident are you now identifying and labeling all sections in a pop song?
Name one thing your formal section map revealed that you had not noticed while just listening casually.
This module practiced pattern recognition (finding structure in complex things). Name one area outside music where recognizing patterns helps you make sense of something complicated.

quizzes.title: Module 26 Intro: Advanced Sight-Singing and Ear Training

questions.text: Essential question: When a melody uses pitches outside the scale, how do you figure out what to sing? Write 2-3 sentences of your first instinct. No wrong answer yet.
This module I will:

answers.text: Learn chromatic solfege syllables for all raised and lowered pitches
Apply a five-step strategy to sight-sing melodies with accidentals
Write down melodies with chromatic pitches using a dictation protocol

questions.text: How comfortable are you sight-singing a diatonic melody right now (no accidentals)? (1 = I need to review | 3 = Somewhat comfortable | 5 = Very comfortable)
The five raised chromatic solfege syllables are:
In the moveable-Do system, F♯ in C major is called:
B♭ in C major is called:
G♯ in C major is called:
E♭ in C major is called:
A♭ in C major is called:
In the five-step sight-singing strategy, what is Step 1?
"Inner hearing" means:

answers.text: singing in your head on a neutral syllable
imagining the sound of written notes before performing them

questions.text: In melodic dictation, what should you do on the FIRST hearing?
True/False: Short daily ear-training sessions (10-15 minutes) build inner hearing faster than one long weekly session.
Essential question revisited: Now that you know chromatic solfege, how has your answer changed? What is the first thing you do when you see an accidental in a melody?
How confident are you now identifying and singing the 10 chromatic solfege syllables? (1 = Not yet confident | 3 = Getting there | 5 = Very confident)
What are the five raised chromatic solfege syllables? What is the vowel rule that unites them?
This module practiced precision, knowing the exact name of a pitch before singing it. Name one place outside music where naming something precisely before acting on it saves you from a mistake.
Essential question: When a piece of music changes key, how does the composer guide you from one tonal center to another? Write 2-3 sentences of your first instinct. No wrong answer yet.
This module I will learn to:

answers.text: Distinguish tonicization from modulation using duration and cadential commitment
Analyze a pivot chord modulation and label the pivot with dual Roman numerals
Identify a direct (chromatic) modulation and explain its expressive effect

questions.text: How comfortable are you identifying secondary dominants and tonicization right now? (1 = I need to review | 3 = Somewhat comfortable | 5 = Very comfortable)
Modulation differs from tonicization because:

answers.text: Modulation uses secondary dominants; tonicization does not
Modulation establishes a new key with a cadence and stays there; tonicization is a brief secondary-dominant visit
Modulation only moves to the dominant; tonicization can go anywhere
Tonicization always changes the key signature

questions.text: The smoothest type of modulation uses a:

answers.text: Direct shift at the phrase boundary
Pivot chord that functions in both keys

questions.text: In a pivot chord modulation from C major to G major, the chord C-E-G functions as:
When labeling a pivot chord, the Roman numeral notation shows:

answers.text: The old-key function above and the new-key function below
The root in both key names
The chord quality and both key names

questions.text: A direct (chromatic) modulation is characterized by:

answers.text: A sudden key change at a phrase boundary with no pivot chord
A held pitch while the harmony shifts
A secondary dominant resolving to a new tonic
A gradual half-step chromatic shift over many measures

questions.text: The "truck-driver" modulation in pop music typically:

answers.text: Raises the final chorus by a half step or whole step
Lowers the final chorus by a step

questions.text: Which keys are most closely related to C major?

answers.text: G major (dominant) and F major (subdominant) and A minor (relative)

questions.text: Common-tone modulation creates what kind of effect?
True/False: A single secondary dominant that resolves back to the original tonic is a modulation.
In a modulation from A minor to C major, the relative major (C major) is reached most smoothly by:

answers.text: A secondary dominant without a pivot
A pivot chord that belongs to both A minor and C major

questions.text: Essential question revisited: Now that you understand modulation, how would you explain the difference between a piece that "visits" another key and one that actually "moves" to a new key? Write 2-3 sentences using the vocabulary from this module.
How confident are you now identifying the three types of modulation (pivot chord, common-tone, direct)? (1 = Not yet confident | 3 = Getting there | 5 = Very confident)
Write out the dual Roman numeral label for the pivot chord in a modulation from C major to F major. Which chord is the pivot, and what are its two functions?

This module explored attentiveness, listening closely enough to hear when a key has genuinely changed versus when it is just visiting. Name one situation outside of music where the difference between "visiting" and "committing" matters.

quizzes.title: Module 28 Intro: Extended Counterpoint and Fugue

questions.text: Essential question: What makes fugal music recognizable even when the same melody appears in different voices, keys, and transformations? Write 2-3 sentences of your first instinct, no wrong answer yet.
This module I will learn to:

answers.text: Write a short imitative counterpoint using a given subject
Identify the subject and answer in a public domain fugal excerpt

questions.text: How confident are you identifying a fugue subject in a piece of music right now? (1 = No idea what to listen for | 3 = Somewhat confident | 5 = Very confident)
The fugal exposition consists of:

answers.text: One voice stating the subject repeatedly
Each voice entering in turn, alternating subject (tonic) and answer (dominant)

questions.text: In a fugue, the "answer" is:

answers.text: The second movement of the fugue
The subject transposed to the dominant key (or an adjusted version of it)

questions.text: What is a countersubject?

answers.text: The main melody of the fugue
A secondary melody that consistently accompanies the subject or answer entries
An episode that follows the exposition

questions.text: An episode in a fugue:

answers.text: States the subject in a new key
Is the same as the exposition
Does not state the subject; uses fragments in sequence; modulates between key areas

questions.text: Stretto is defined as:

answers.text: Subject entries that overlap, a new voice enters before the previous entry finishes
Doubling the note values of the subject

questions.text: Augmentation of a fugue subject means:

answers.text: Cutting all note values in half

questions.text: Inversion of a fugue subject means:

answers.text: Stating it in a different key
Reversing all intervals, rising becomes falling, falling becomes rising

questions.text: A real answer is:

answers.text: A modified transposition that adjusts intervals
An exact transposition of the subject up a perfect fifth

questions.text: Stretto typically appears:

answers.text: Near the end, where overlapping entries create climax

questions.text: Bach's fugues in the Well-Tempered Clavier are:

answers.text: Public domain and freely available on IMSLP

Coloristic, because it establishes the mode without creating dominant-tonic tension
